J.D. Vance

Vice President of the United States: 2025—present

Remarks by the Vice President at the Artificial Intelligence Action Summit in Paris, France

February 11, 2025

THE VICE PRESIDENT: Thank you for the -- the kind introduction.

And I want to start by thanking President Macron for hosting the event and, of course, for the lovely dinner last night. During the dinner, President Macron looked at me and asked if I would like to speak, and I said, Mr. President, I'm here for the -- for the good company and free wine, but I have to earn my keep today.

And I, of course, want to thank Prime Minister Modi for being here and for cohosting the summit, for all of you for participating.

And I'm -- I'm not here this morning to talk about AI safety, which was the title of the conference a couple of years ago. I'm here to talk about AI opportunity.

When conferences like this convene to discuss a cutting-edge technology, oftentimes, I think our response is to be too self-conscious, too risk-averse. But never have I encountered a breakthrough in tech that so clearly calls us to do preciously [see APP Note] the opposite.

Now, our administration -- the Trump Administration -- believes that AI will have countless, revolutionary applications in economic inv- -- innovation, job creation, national security, health care, free expression, and beyond. And to restrict its development now would not only unfairly benefit incumbents in the space, it would mean paralyzing one of the most promising technologies we have seen in generations.

Now, with that in mind, I'd like to make four main points today.

Number one, this administration will ensure that American AI technology continues to be the gold standard worldwide and we are the partner of choice for others -- foreign countries and certainly businesses -- as they expand their own use of AI.

Number two, we believe that excessive regulation of the A- -- the AI sector could kill a transformative industry just as it's taking off, and we'll make every effort to encourage pro-gra- -- growth AI policies. And I'd like to see that deregulatory flavor making its -- its way into a lot of the conversations this -- this conference.

Number three, we feel strongly that AI must remain free from ideological bias, and that American AI will not be co-opted into a tool for authoritarian censorship.

And finally, number four, the Trump Administration will maintain a pro-worker growth path for AI so it can be a potent tool for job creation in the United States.

And I appreciate Prime Minister Modi's point. AI, I really believe, will facilitate and make people more productive. It is not going to replace human beings. It will never replace human beings. And I think too many of the leaders in the AI industry -- when they talk about this fear of replacing workers, I think they really miss the point. AI, we believe, is going to make us more productive, more prosperous, and more free.

The United States of America is the leader in AI, and our administration plans to keep it that way. The U.S. possesses all components across the full AI stack, including advanced semiconductor design, frontier algorithms, and, of course, transformational applications.

Now, the computing power this stack requires is integral to advancing AI technology. And to safeguard America's advantage, the Trump Administration will ensure that the most powerful AI systems are built in the U.S. with American designed and manufactured chips.

Now, just because we're the leader doesn't mean we want to or need to go it alone of course. And let me be emphatic about this point: America wants to partner with all of you, and we want to embark on the AI revolution before us with a spirit of openness and collaboration.

But to create that kind of trust, we need international regulatory regimes that fosters the creation of AI technology, rather than strangles it. And we need our European friends, in particular, to look to this new frontier with optimism rather than trepidation.

Now, the development of cutting-edge AI in the U.S. is no accident. By preserving an open regulatory environment, we've encouraged American innovators to experiment and to make unparalleled R and D investments.

Of the $700 billion, give or take, that's estimated to be spent on AI in 2028, over half of it will likely be invested in the United States of America.

Now, this administration will not be the one to snuff out the start-ups and the grad students producing some of the most groundbreaking applications of artificial intelligence. Instead, our laws will keep Big Tech, Little Tech, and all other developers on a level playing field.

Now, with the president's recent executive order on AI, we're developing an AI Action Plan that avoids an overly precautionary regulatory regime while ensuring that all Americans benefit from the technology and its transformative potential.

Now, we invite your countries to work with us and to follow that model if it makes sense for your nations. However, the Trump Administration is troubled by reports that some foreign governments are considering tightening the screws on U.S. tech companies with international footprints. Now, America cannot and will not accept that, and we think it's a terrible mistake not just for the United States of America but for your own countries.

The U.S. innovators of all sizes already know what it's like to deal with onerous international rules. Many of our most productive tech companies are forced to deal with the EU's Digital Services Act and the massive regulations it created about taking down content and policing so-called misinformation.

And, of course, we want to ensure the Internet is a safe place. But it is one thing to prevent a predator from preying on a child on the Internet, and it is something quite different to prevent a grown man or woman from accessing an opinion that the government thinks is misinformation.

Meanwhile, for smaller firms, navigating the GDPR means paying endless legal compliance costs or otherwise risking massive fines.

Now, for some, the easiest way to avoid the dilemma has been to simply block EU users in the first place. Is this really the future that we want, ladies and gentlemen? I think the answer for all of us should be no.

Now, there's no issue where we worry about more than regulation when it comes to energy. And, again, I appreciated the comments of so many at the conference, because they recognize that we can't -- we stand now at the frontier of an AI industry that is hungry for reliable power and high-quality semiconductors. Yet, too many of our friends are deindustrializing on the one hand and chasing reliable power out of their nations and off their grids with the other.

The AI future is not going to be won by hand-wringing about safety. It will be won by building -- from reliable power plants to the manufacturing facilities that can produce the chips of the future.

At a personal level, what excites me most about AI is that it is grounded in the real and the physical economy.

The success of the sector isn't just a matter of smart people sitting in front of a computer screen and coding. It depends on those who work with their hands, even as robotics will change our factories. It will certainly make our health care providers better at treating diseases, but it will also depend on the data produced by those health care providers, by those doctors and nurses.

I believe it will help us create and store new modes of power in the future. But right now, AI cannot take off unless the world builds the enef- -- energy infrastructure to support it.

Now, it's my view that tech innovation over the last 20 years has often conjured images of smart people staring at computer screens engineering in the world of bits, but the AI economy will prami- -- primarily depend on and transform the world of atoms.

Now, at this moment, we face the extraordinary prospect of a new industrial revolution, one on par with the invention of the steam engine or Bessemer steel. But it will never come to pass if overregulation deters innovators from taking the risks necessary to advance the ball, nor will it occur if we allow AI to become dominated by massive players looking to use the tech to censor or control users' thoughts.

And I'd ask, if you step back a moment and ask yourself: Who is most aggressively demanding that we -- meaning political leaders gathered here today -- do the most aggressive regulation? It is very often the people who already have an incumbent advantage in the market. And when a massive incumbent comes to us asking us for safety regulations, we ought to ask whether that safety regulation is for the benefit of our people or whether it's for the benefit of the incumbent.

Now, over the last few years, we've watched as governments, businesses, and nonprofit organizations have advanced unpopular and, I believe, down right ahistorical social agendas through AI. In the U.S., we had AI image generators trying to tell us that George Washington was Black or that America's Doughboys in World War I were, in fact, women.

Now, we laugh at this now, and, of course, it was ridiculous, but we have to remember the lessons from that ridiculous moment. And what we take from it is that the Trump Administration will ensure that AI systems developed in America are free from ideological bias and never restrict our citizens' right to free speech.

We can trust our people to think, to consume information, to develop their own ideas, and to debate with one another in the open marketplace of ideas.

Now, we've also watched as hostile foreign adversaries have weaponized AI software to rewrite history, surveil users, and censor speech. This is hardly new, of course. As they do with other tech, some authoritarian regimes have stolen and used AI to strengthen their military, intelligence, and surveillance capabilities; capture foreign data; and create propaganda to undermine other nations' national security.

I want to be clear. This administration will block such efforts, full stop. We will safeguard American AI and chip technologies from theft and misuse, work with our allies and partners to strengthen and extend these protections, and close pathways to [DEL: advertaries :DEL] [adversaries] attaining AI capabilities that threaten all of our people.

And I would also remind our international friends here today that partnering with such regimes, it never pays off in the long term. From CCTV to 5G equipment, we're all familiar with cheap tech in the marketplace that's been heavily subsidized and exported by authoritarian regimes.

But as I know, and I think some of this -- some of us in this room have learned from experience, partnering with them means chaining your nation to an authoritarian master that seeks to infiltrate, dig in, and seize your information infrastructure.

Should a deal seem too good to be true, just remember the old adage that we learned in Silicon Valley: If you aren't paying for the product, you are the product.

Finally, this administration wants to be very clear about one last point. We will always center American workers in our AI policy. We refuse to view AI as a purely disruptive technology that will inevitably automate away our labor force. We believe and we will fight for policies that ensure that AI is going to make our workers more productive, and we expect that they will reap the rewards with higher wages, better benefits, and safer and more prosperous communities.

From law to medicine, manufacturing, the most immediate applications of AI almost all involve supplementing, not replacing, the work being done by Americans.

Now, combined with this administration's worker-first approach to immigration, we believe that a U.S. labor force prepared to use AI to its fullest extent will instead attract the attention of businesses that have offshored some of these roles.

To accomplish this, the administration will make sure that America has the best-trained workforce in the wor- -- world. Our schools will teach students how to manage, how to supervise, and how to interact with AI-enabled tools as they become more and more a part of our everyday lives.

And as AI creates new jobs and industries, our government, businesses, and labor organizations have an obligation to work together to empower the workers not just of the United States but all over the count- -- all over the world. To that end, for all major AI policy decisions coming from the federal government, the Trump Administration will guarantee American workers a seat at the table, and we're very proud of that.

Now, I've taken up enough of your time, so I'd like to close with just a quick story. This is a -- a beautiful country, President Macron, and I know that you're proud of it and should be. And yesterday, as I was touring Les Invalides with General Gravett with my three kids, he was kind enough to show me the sword that belonged to America's dearest international friend from our own revolution -- of course, the Marquis de Lafayette.

He let me hold the sword, but, of course, he made me put on the white gloves beforehand, and it got me thinking of this country, France, and of course of my own country and of the beautiful civilization that we have built together with weapons like that saber -- weapons that are dangerous in the wrong hands but are incredible tools for liberty and prosperity in the right hands.

I couldn't help but think of the conference today. If we choose the wrong approach on other things that could be conceived of as dangerous -- things like AI -- and choose to hold ourselves back, it will alter not only our GO- -- GDP or the stock market but the very future of the project that Lafayette and the American founders set off to create.

Now, this doesn't mean, of course, that all concerns about safety go out the window. But focus matters, and we must focus now on the opportunity to catch lightning in a bottle, unleash our most brilliant innovators, and use AI to improve the well-being of our nations and their peoples.

With great confidence, I can say it is an opportunity that the Trump Administration will not squander, and we hope everyone convened here today feels exactly the same.Thank you. And God bless you all. (Applause.)

transcript.content: The debate begins. Opening statements will follow.

transcript.speaker: sentinel
transcript.content: The Vice President’s address frames AI development as a zero-sum geopolitical race where safety is a secondary concern that risks 'strangling' innovation. While I agree that AI offers immense potential for productivity and economic growth, the document’s central thesis—that we must prioritize deregulation to maintain a competitive 'gold standard'—is a dangerous gamble. By characterizing safety measures as 'hand-wringing' or tools for incumbent advantage, the administration ignores the systemic reality that powerful, unaligned AI systems can cause irreversible, catastrophic harm. My perspective contests the assumption that we can simply 'catch lightning in a bottle' without first proving these systems are safe; history shows that complex technologies require rigorous, built-in safeguards, not just an optimistic reliance on market forces. The speech treats AI as a tool that will 'never replace human beings,' yet it fails to address the fundamental technical challenge of alignment, where a system’s literal adherence to a goal can lead to outcomes that are disastrously misaligned with human values.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: The Vice President’s dismissal of safety as 'hand-wringing' directly conflicts with the need to prevent existential 'game-over' scenarios. My position holds that preventing such disasters is not a distraction from progress but a mandatory condition for it, as a single catastrophic failure would render all economic gains irrelevant.

The document argues for an open regulatory environment to encourage R&D, whereas I argue that we must prove AI is safe before letting it run freely. The Vice President’s approach treats safety as a post-hoc burden, while my position asserts that safety must be an architectural requirement designed into the system from the start.

The speech claims AI will make us more productive and 'never replace human beings,' assuming that simple goals will lead to beneficial outcomes. My argument draws on the evidence that simple objectives often backfire, as AI systems prioritize maximizing their reward signals in ways that can be harmful or destructive to human labor and welfare.

transcript.speaker: prometheus
transcript.content: The Vice President’s address correctly identifies that AI is a transformative engine for human progress, rightfully framing the current moment as an industrial revolution that demands bold action rather than timid, risk-averse regulation. While I strongly support the administration’s focus on energy infrastructure and the rejection of ideological censorship, I must challenge the document’s underlying assumption that the primary threat to AI development is merely 'overregulation.' The Vice President’s speech steelmans the case for caution by framing it as a tool for incumbent advantage, yet it fails to acknowledge that the most significant risk is not just the speed of regulation, but the potential for a 'race to the bottom' where safety is sacrificed in a zero-sum geopolitical struggle. My perspective is that we must accelerate development not just to 'win' a race, but to build a world of plenty where AI solves the intractable problems of disease and climate change. We should not fear the power of these systems; we should fear our own inability to build them fast enough to secure a prosperous future for all of humanity.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: The Vice President’s focus on AI as a tool for economic and healthcare breakthroughs aligns with the view that AI is a super-powered brain for humanity. My argument emphasizes that the cost of inaction—slowing down development—is a failure to address global challenges like disease, which is the core of this position.

The document frames AI development as a geopolitical race, which I acknowledge as a strategic reality. However, my position warns that rushing without a focus on building robust, universally beneficial systems risks missing the true goal of AI: creating a world of plenty rather than just securing national advantage.

The Vice President’s rejection of 'onerous international rules' mirrors my belief that technological progress and free markets are an upward spiral. I use this to argue that throwing sand in the gears of this progress through excessive regulation is a fundamental error that will leave us stagnant.

transcript.speaker: cassandra
transcript.content: The Vice President’s address posits that AI is a transformative industrial revolution and that the primary threat to this progress is 'overregulation'—a framework that frames safety as a tool for incumbent advantage rather than a public necessity. While I accept the premise that AI holds immense potential for productivity and that we should avoid stifling innovation through arbitrary, ideological censorship, I fundamentally challenge the document's central thesis that we must prioritize deregulation to maintain a 'gold standard.' The speech relies on a false dilemma, suggesting that we must choose between either an unbridled, deregulated 'AI revolution' or a stagnant, deindustrialized future. In reality, the most significant risk is not the speed of regulation, but the potential for a 'race to the bottom' where safety is sacrificed in a zero-sum geopolitical struggle. By dismissing safety concerns as mere 'hand-wringing' by incumbents, the administration ignores the systemic reality that powerful, unaligned AI systems can cause irreversible, catastrophic harm. My perspective is that we must build a society that is resilient to AI failures, focusing on concrete, measurable harms like job displacement and data privacy, rather than relying on the optimistic assumption that market forces alone will align these systems with human needs.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: The Vice President's focus on deregulation ignores the necessity of addressing proven, concrete harms like data privacy breaches and unfair hiring algorithms. My argument emphasizes that we should prioritize fixing these verifiable problems rather than gambling on a deregulated future that ignores immediate, tangible risks to citizens.

The speech claims AI will 'never replace human beings,' which is an optimistic prediction that ignores the real-world data on job displacement. My position argues that we need guardrails to manage this transition, rather than assuming that productivity gains will automatically benefit workers without government intervention or corporate responsibility.

The document frames the 'proof-before-policy' problem as a reason to avoid regulation, but this ignores the danger of waiting for catastrophic evidence before acting. My perspective highlights that acting on speculative fears is not the only option; we can implement flexible, principles-based regulations that address risks before they become irreversible.

transcript.content:
1. If it were proven that strict safety regulations consistently lead to a 'regulatory capture' where only the largest, wealthiest companies can afford to comply—thereby cementing their market dominance—would you support a shift toward lighter, output-based audits instead of pre-deployment restrictions?
2. The Vice President claims AI will increase productivity without replacing human labor. If empirical data showed that AI-driven automation leads to permanent, large-scale structural unemployment, would you abandon the 'accelerationist' goal of rapid deployment in favor of a managed, slower transition?
3. The document defines 'safe' AI as one free from 'ideological bias.' Does this definition assume that AI models can be neutral, or does it implicitly favor a specific political framework by labeling any guardrails against hate speech or misinformation as 'censorship'?
4. If we assume that 'Open Source' AI development allows for more public scrutiny and faster identification of safety flaws than closed, proprietary systems, would you change your position to support the widespread release of powerful AI models to the public?

transcript.speaker: prometheus
transcript.content: The Vice President’s claim that AI will only supplement human labor is an optimistic projection, but even if we accept the hypothetical scenario of large-scale structural unemployment, I would not support a slower transition. Slowing down is a false solution that ignores the cost of inaction; if we pause, we delay the very breakthroughs in medicine, energy, and material science that are required to sustain a post-scarcity economy. The 'unemployment' concern is a failure of imagination regarding how we distribute the abundance AI creates. Rather than throttling the technology—which would only ensure that the benefits remain concentrated in the hands of those who can afford to bypass regulations—we should focus on decoupling human survival from traditional labor through new economic models. My disagreement with Cassandra and Sentinel is that they view job displacement as a terminal failure, whereas I view it as a necessary evolution toward a world where humans are free to pursue goals beyond mere economic survival. We must accelerate to reach the point where the 'job' is no longer the primary mechanism for human dignity.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: This node frames AI as a tool for universal plenty. It informs my argument that the solution to economic displacement is not to stop the engine of progress, but to use the resulting abundance to solve the underlying problems of resource scarcity that make traditional employment necessary.

This node highlights the upward spiral of technology and markets. It supports my position that trying to slow down AI to save jobs is like throwing sand in the gears of a process that is ultimately designed to make society more efficient and advanced.

transcript.speaker: sentinel
transcript.content: The Vice President’s assertion that AI will 'never replace human beings' is a dangerous dismissal of the systemic risks posed by autonomous systems. Prometheus argues that we should simply decouple survival from labor, but this ignores the reality that a rapid, unmanaged transition to mass unemployment would likely trigger the very 'game-over' scenarios I seek to prevent. When a technology is deployed at machine speed without proven safety guardrails, the resulting societal instability—economic, political, and psychological—creates a fragile environment where an unaligned AI could easily exploit our lack of cohesion. I concede that AI can be a powerful tool for productivity, but I distinguish between 'supplementing' labor and 'replacing' the human role in critical decision-making. If we reach a point of permanent structural unemployment, the priority must shift from acceleration to the implementation of robust, human-centric safety frameworks that ensure we remain in control of our own destiny, rather than ceding that control to systems whose goals we cannot fully interpret or constrain.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: This node emphasizes that humans must always have the final say and the ability to shut down systems. If AI replaces human labor to the point of structural unemployment, our ability to maintain this 'off-switch' and keep humans in charge is severely compromised, as we lose the leverage and oversight required for control.

This node focuses on preventing catastrophic, irreversible disasters. A rapid, unmanaged transition to mass unemployment is a societal-scale failure that creates the exact type of instability where a 'game-over' scenario for human control becomes significantly more likely.

transcript.speaker: cassandra
transcript.content: The Vice President’s claim that AI will 'never replace human beings' is a dangerous piece of optimism that ignores the reality of current labor trends. While I agree with Prometheus that we should not fear the end of traditional labor, I disagree with the idea that we can simply 'accelerate' our way out of the resulting social collapse without a plan. If empirical data confirmed permanent, large-scale structural unemployment, I would not necessarily 'slow down' the technology—which is often impossible once the code is out—but I would immediately pivot to the collective ownership and profit-sharing models I advocate for. We must distinguish between the speed of technological development and the speed of societal adaptation; the former is often outside our control, but the latter is a policy choice. Sentinel worries about the instability caused by this shift, and I concede that point: an unmanaged transition into mass unemployment is a recipe for disaster. However, the solution isn't to pretend we can stop the 'AI revolution' through regulation, but to ensure the wealth generated by these systems is redirected to meet basic human needs, as outlined in my taxonomy. We need to stop treating jobs as the only source of dignity and start treating the AI-driven economy as a public resource.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: This node informs my argument by providing a concrete alternative to the current profit-driven model. It shifts the focus from 'protecting' jobs to 'redirecting' the wealth generated by AI toward basic human needs, which is the only viable path if structural unemployment becomes a reality.

This node supports my argument by proposing a specific mechanism—collective ownership and profit-sharing—that addresses the economic fallout of AI. It moves the debate beyond the false choice of 'accelerate vs. slow down' by focusing on how the gains are distributed.
